name: BoolQ
description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer (yes or no). The questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and are paired with Wikipedia passages. The dataset contains 16,000 examples split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
publisher: Google AI Language / University of Washington
citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044.
rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator for further processing. Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) deciding if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information), (2) finding a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and (3) marking whether the answer is yes or no. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are included in the dataset.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were incorporated.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions from the NQ training set with yes/no answers were incorporated into the dataset and are always placed in the train set. The dataset is split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set. Each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries are heuristically filtered to identify likely yes/no questions by checking if the first word belongs to a manually constructed set of indicator words and if the query is of sufficient length. Only queries where a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results are kept. Annotators further filter by marking questions as 'good' or not, and mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Only questions with a yes/no answer are retained.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) they decide if the question is 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; (2) for good questions, they find a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question, and can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information; (3) they mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Annotation quality was assessed by having three of the authors label 110 randomly chosen examples, conferring on disagreements to produce gold-standard labels.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to produce gold-standard labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Due to sufficiently high agreement, singly-annotated examples were used in the training/dev/test sets.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated examples used in training/dev/test sets; 3 authors annotated a subset of 110 examples for quality assessment)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has been noted to have been updated since some analyses were carried out (the inference type analysis may be slightly out-of-date). No formal versioning or deprecation policy is described.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, which has real-world applications in question answering systems and search engines.
rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The dataset was noted to have potential annotation artifacts, though the questions themselves are naturally occurring rather than crowd-sourced, which helps mitigate some annotation biases. Questions from NQ are always placed in the train set, which may introduce some distribution differences between splits.
rai:dataLimitations: The inference type analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset has been updated since that analysis was carried out. The dataset contains singly-annotated examples, which may introduce some label noise (approximately 10% disagreement with gold-standard labels). The dataset is class-imbalanced with 62.31% yes answers. The article title is included but none of the presented models make use of it.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, development, and testing of reading comprehension and natural language inference models, specifically for yes/no question answering. It can be used to evaluate a model's ability to make complex inferences from text. The authors also use it as a target dataset for transfer learning experiments.
